newsitem.title: KUWAIT: U.S. seeks support for arms buildup against Iraq.
newsitem.headline: U.S. seeks support for arms buildup against Iraq.

text.p: A U.S. military buildup continued in the Gulf on Monday with Defence Secretary William Perry warning Iraq's leader Saddam Hussein to stop deploying anti-aircraft missile batteries in the extended southern Iraqi no-fly zone.
Kuwait, the only Middle East country to endorse U.S. missile attacks on Iraq earlier this month, formally approved Washington's plan to send up to 5,000 ground troops to the country bordering Iraq.

The U.S. submarine Pittsburgh waited to pass through the Suez Canal on Tuesday evening to join the American forces in the Gulf facing Iraqi President Saddam Hussein, port officials said. It is armed with Tomahawk cruise missiles like those used to attack southern Iraq earlier this month.

The U.S. aircraft carrier Enterprise passed through the canal on Sunday to join the carrier Carl Vinson in the Gulf. Together they carry 150 warplanes. U.S. B-52 long-range bombers had already been moved within striking distance on the Indian Ocean base of Diego Garcia.

Despite the preparations, an American attack appeared increasingly uncertain in the face of an Iraqi retreat from confrontation and a dearth of diplomatic support for U.S. President Bill Clinton's tough line toward Saddam.
The United States has found little apparent enthusiasm among members of the old Gulf War coalition for further attacks on Iraq. Some members have expressed serious doubts about U.S. bombing raids.

Perry, returning from a trip to Turkey and the Gulf where he sought support from U.S. allies for the buildup, said in London that Saddam had to halt "aggressive deployment" of mobile surface-to-air missiles in the south that threatened U.S. planes.

"All of these actions we find threatening, we find provoking and we find necessary to change," Perry said after briefing British Defence Secretary Michael Portillo and French Defence Minister Charles Millon on his talks in Turkey and the Gulf.
Millon pointed up differences in the old Gulf War coalition by warning his American and British counterparts against an escalation of the crisis, according to a French defence ministry statement.

He said France was concerned over the safety of its pilots enforcing the no-fly zone over Iraq together with British and U.S. aviators, but the statement said France believed that any threat against allied planes should be answered by "a proportional response".

"We have sought no confrontation with Saddam Hussein," Clinton said when asked about the likelihood of another U.S. attack. But he carefully avoided saying if the prospects of further fighting had changed.
Perry received little obvious support in Turkey on a swing through the region to restore the coalition that drove Saddam's occupation troops from Kuwait in 1991.
Clinton, facing a presidential election in less than two months, ordered the buildup last week after Iraq fired on U.S. planes in no-fly zones.

However, Iraq, which precipitated the crisis at the end of August by sending troops into Kurdish northern Iraq -- also closed to Saddam's forces for the past five years -- announced last Friday it would suspend attacks on western air patrols.
Clinton came under criticism at home from Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole for inflicting only "pinpricks" on Iraq instead of real punishment. But abroad the view was mainly the opposite.
In Turkey, which provided bases in the Gulf War and lets Washington use the Incirlik airbase to patrol northern Iraq, Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller told Perry it would not help in a new attack.
Iran on Monday sought U.N. aid for 60,000 Iraqi Kurds who had fled after the Baghdad-backed Kurdish militia conquered northern Iraq. U.N. officials had reported about 30,000.
Other refugees, who worked for U.S. organisations in northern Iraq, would be taken via Turkey to the Pacific island of Guam en route to the United States, a U.S. diplomat said.
